page_title: Choosing an HTTP Status Code — Stop Making It Hard

sources.entry: Choosing an HTTP Status Code — Stop Making It Hard

summary.title: Choosing an HTTP Status Code — Stop Making It Hard
summary.one_liner: A practical guide, built around a flowchart, for picking the right HTTP status code for a website or REST-style API, plus an argument for why specific codes still matter.
takeaways: Pick a status code by first choosing its response class (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx); if you are choosing between codes in different classes, you are likely wrong.
Use 301 vs 302 deliberately: 301 has SEO implications and is implicitly cacheable, while 302 does not carry those implications.
Distinguish 404 from 405 Method Not Allowed, and 502 Bad Gateway (upstream failure) from 500 Internal Server Error.
Follow the emerging convention of returning 201 Created, 429 Too Many Requests and 503 Service Unavailable so clients can handle them meaningfully.
The author cites RFC 7231 as the current HTTP/1.1 semantics reference, not the older RFC 2616 or 2068.
summary.summary: The author argues that choosing HTTP status codes should be simple and offers a flowchart-based approach for websites and RESTish APIs, grouping codes into 2XX/3XX, 4XX and 5XX categories. He points to RFC 7231 as the authoritative reference and notes that the older RFC 2616 is superseded. A coda questions whether specific codes matter, citing an API that only returns 200, and then gives three reasons they still do: clients can handle codes with special behavior (such as 301 caching and 429 backoff), some codes deserve special handling, and a convention for codes like 201, 429 and 503 is emerging. The flowcharts themselves are images and are not described in the page text.
